Steel case is fine, just don't mix without cleaning. Switching between steel and brass will cause the brass cases to stick in the chamber. Lacquer is used on the steel case and leaves residue in the chamber. There is also accelerated wear to parts such as extractors with steel case ammo. This coupled with the fact that most steel cased ammo is dirtier are the biggest downsides. However considering how much cheaper it is to buy steel cased ammo in bulk, in most cases this savings offsets or covers the repairs of the parts that wear.

Lead in itself will not mess up your gun. Most bullets are lead. Only boutique ammo is typically made of other material. If you mean only use coated, bonded or plated bullets, this depends on what you are doing and what the lead is composed of. For example, a Glock has octagonal rifling. This is prone to lead fouling compared to normal rifling. If using this rifling you should stay away from pure lead bullets. When using lead bullets, the biggest things to take into account is proper sizing to your barrel and speed of the bullet. If the bullet is not fit tight gasses cut past the bullet while it is traveling down the barrel causing lead fouling. If too tight, excess pressure is made. Above certain speeds the lead bullet does not maintain itself. This is what the coatings on most modern bullets fight. They allow improper sizing, and higher speeds. If you want to see the limits of what a lead bullet can do you should look at reloading handbooks and guides, .357 and .44 mag will most likely have the most information on this as they are very popular.
